subChunks.title: Adapter & Decorator

storyBeats.text: Eldrin adapts an ancient dusty spell book to work with the modern Academy's casting interface — without rewriting the book.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The Adapter pattern is the universal translator. When the interface of an existing class doesn't match what you need, you wrap it in an Adapter that speaks both languages. The old code is untouched; the new code sees only the interface it expects.

storyBeats.label: Decorator chain

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Decorator adds behaviour without subclassing. Stack as many decorators as you need — each wraps the previous. Java I/O streams are a classic example: new BufferedReader(new FileReader(file)) — each layer adds capability.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Implement an Adapter: OldPrinter has printOld(String). New code expects Printer interface with print(String). Create PrinterAdapter and verify it works.
guidedPractice.hint: PrinterAdapter holds an OldPrinter instance and delegates print() to printOld().

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the Adapter pattern. Give a real-world example of when you would use it.

questions.prompt: What problem does the Decorator pattern solve that inheritance cannot?
options: Adding behaviour dynamically at runtime without subclassing
Hiding the implementation from the caller
questions.answer: Adding behaviour dynamically at runtime without subclassing
questions.explanation: Decorator wraps objects at runtime — you can combine multiple decorators in any order. Inheritance is static (compile-time), and deep inheritance hierarchies become rigid and brittle.

subChunks.title: Facade & Proxy

storyBeats.text: Eldrin creates a single 'Start Academy Day' lever. Behind it: locking the vault, raising the bridge, lighting the torches, summoning the staff — seven subsystems. Clients pull one lever.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The Facade is a simple door into a complex room. Clients interact only with the facade; the complexity of the subsystem is hidden. The subsystem classes still exist and can be used directly when needed — the facade just provides a convenient entry point.

storyBeats.label: Proxy for caching

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Proxy is a gatekeeper. It stands in front of a real object, intercepting calls to add behaviour: caching, logging, access control, lazy loading. Spring AOP creates proxies automatically for @Transactional and @Cacheable methods.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Implement a SpellcastingFacade with a castSpell() method that calls ManaSystem.check(), ArcaneChannel.open(), and prints "Spell cast!".
guidedPractice.hint: The facade creates instances of ManaSystem and ArcaneChannel internally and delegates to them.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: What is the difference between Facade and Adapter patterns? When would you use a Proxy pattern?

questions.prompt: Spring's @Transactional annotation works by wrapping your bean in a ________?
questions.explanation: Spring creates a proxy around @Transactional beans. The proxy intercepts method calls, starts/commits/rolls back transactions, then delegates to the real bean. This is the Proxy pattern in action.
